_about: Everything built and everything we could add, on one list and one map.

categories.cross-national: Same instrument fielded in several countries.
categories.economics/behavioural: Risk, money, time preference, economic judgement.
categories.political identity/polarisation: How people regard each other across a political divide — the outcome is a judgement of a person.
categories.political preferences/policy: What people want government to do — the outcome is a judgement of a policy.
categories.survey methodology: The instrument itself is the object of study.
categories.work/family/gender: Employment, caregiving, gender and family roles.

rows.title: Divided by the Vote: Affective Polarization in the Wake of the Brexit Referendum (BBC conjoint)
rows.description: Forced choice between two applicants for Director General of the BBC, described by name, age, experience, degree, party politics, EU referendum vote and occupation. Tests whether Leave/Remain identity affects judgement of competence for a public role.
rows.nearest_built_title: Divided by the Vote: Affective Polarization in the Wake of the Brexit Referendum (Lodger conjoint)

rows.title: Divided by the Vote: Affective Polarization in the Wake of the Brexit Referendum (Lodger conjoint)
rows.description: Forced choice between two prospective lodgers described by name, age, occupation, volunteering, party politics, EU referendum vote and hobby. The classic social-distance measure: would you share your home with someone who voted the other way.
rows.nearest_built_title: Divided by the Vote: Affective Polarization in the Wake of the Brexit Referendum (BBC conjoint)

rows.title: Divided by the Vote: Affective Polarization in the Wake of the Brexit Referendum (Sky emotional attachment battery)
rows.description: Five-item battery measuring strength of emotional attachment to one's own Brexit identity (Leaver/Remainer) or party identity (Conservative/Labour) — in-group language, personal offence at criticism, felt commonality, connectedness and pride in one's own side. The in-group-identification component of affective polarization, restricted to respondents with a clean primary identity (excludes 'Neither'/'None' respondents routed into a battery via an undocumented follow-up question).

rows.title: Pricing Immigration
rows.description: Respondents are told the government will, after Brexit, either keep immigration at roughly current levels or only cut it a little while shifting its source from Europe to beyond Europe. Two outcomes under whichever scenario they met: which party they would support in the next general election, and how satisfied they would feel about the Brexit decision. Tests whether the SOURCE of post-Brexit immigration, not just its level, moves party support and Brexit satisfaction.
rows.nearest_built_title: Pricing Immigration

rows.title: Pricing Immigration
rows.description: Respondents are asked what percentage of all immigrants to the UK they would like to see coming from the EU (vs. elsewhere), on a 0-100 slider; half are additionally told the current EU share is 50%. Tests whether an explicit base-rate anchor shifts the preferred EU/non-EU immigration mix.

rows.title: Mind the Gap: Why Wealthy Voters Support Brexit
rows.description: Respondents are told to imagine they have won a substantial lottery prize, or told nothing, then asked how satisfied they are that the UK voted to leave the EU. Tests whether unearned wealth shifts Brexit support.
rows.nearest_built_title: Mind the Gap: Why Wealthy Voters Support Brexit

rows.title: Mind the Gap: Why Wealthy Voters Support Brexit

rows.title: Citizens from 13 countries share similar preferences for COVID-19 vaccine allocation priorities
rows.description: Forced choice between two hypothetical people over who should receive a COVID-19 vaccine first, differing on risk of death, risk of transmitting, income, occupation and age. A rationing problem: who deserves a scarce life-saving good.
rows.nearest_built_title: Perceptions of Diversity Across Groups

rows.title: Replication Data for: The Variable Persuasiveness of Political Rhetoric
rows.description: Respondents see two of 336 political arguments (14 rhetorical elements x 12 policy issues x 2 positions, for/against) shown together, verbatim as extracted from Hansard debate transcripts, and say which they find more persuasive or that the two are about the same. The respondent judges which ARGUMENT about a policy is persuasive, not a person — closer to the 'policy' pole than the 'identity' pole, since nothing about Leave/Remain regard for other people is measured. Unlike every other UK Dataverse study in this corpus (all conjoints, where the condition is a table of attribute levels this project renders into prose), the condition text here is the fielded instrument's own argument text, transcribed verbatim and not authored by this project.
rows.nearest_built_title: For and Against Brexit: A Survey Experiment of the Impact of Campaign Effects on Public Attitudes toward EU Membership

rows.title: For and Against Brexit: A Survey Experiment of the Impact of Campaign Effects on Public Attitudes toward EU Membership
rows.description: Respondents are shown a campaign vignette combining a pro- or anti-EU cultural frame, a pro- or anti-EU economic frame and a pro- or anti-EU political frame (eight combinations), or no vignette at all (a true control), then asked how they would vote in the EU membership referendum. Tests which real-world campaign arguments, alone and in combination, shift referendum vote intention.
rows.nearest_built_title: Policy Preferences and Policy Legitimacy After Referendums: Evidence from the Brexit Negotiations

rows.title: A Tale of Two Peoples: Motivated Reasoning in the Aftermath of the Brexit Vote
rows.description: A split ballot crossing a Leaver/Remainer identity prime with factual information about UK GDP growth. Outcomes are the respondent's estimate of the UK's growth rank among 34 OECD countries, and whether they think the economy is getting better or worse. Tests motivated reasoning about shared economic facts.

rows.title: Support for digitising the ballot box: a systematic review of i-voting pilots and a conjoint experiment
rows.description: Forced choice between two hypothetical UK internet-voting (i-voting) policies, differing on ten features — pre-registration, voting method, voting window, where trials succeeded, the pilot's effect on turnout and on fraud risk, who controls the platform, the cost to government, the proposing party and the endorsing body. The respondent judges a PROPOSED POLICY, not a person.

rows.title: Alcohol consumption
rows.description: Respondents who had drunk alcohol in the past year report how much they drink on a typical drinking day and how often they binge, with the questions worded in UNITS of alcohol (the NHS version) or in ALCOHOLIC DRINKS. The binge threshold is 6 or more for women and 8 or more for men. The rows teach whether the same person reports differently when asked in units, which few people count in. Wave 15 (2022).

The condition is whether they had already been asked the existing Understanding Society caring questions earlier in the interview. Wave 17 (2024).

rows.title: Measuring sexual identity using direct and indirect questioning
rows.description: Respondents see six lists of statements about who they have been attracted to, who they have had a sexual experience with, and how they would describe themselves, and report only HOW MANY are true for them. Three of the lists carry one extra, sensitive statement ('is the same sex as me'; 'gay, lesbian or bisexual'), a technique for measuring what people will not say directly. Wave 8 (2015).

rows.title: What do the general population regard as “successful ageing”?
rows.description: Respondents read three descriptions of an imaginary 75-year-old and rate how successfully each is ageing, 0-10. Six life dimensions are randomised per description -- long-term illness (none or diabetes), difficulty climbing stairs, problems remembering, opening food packaging, how often they see family and friends, and volunteering -- and the name (George, Harry, Margaret or Anne), which sets the pronouns and is named in the question. The respondent judges ANOTHER person, so the outcome is social perception of ageing, not self-report. Wave 17 (2024). Wording identical to wave 9 but for one comma.

rows.title: Vignettes: measuring flexibility stigma - double whammy or femininity stigma
rows.description: Respondents in work, aged 18-65, imagine they are an HR manager filling a full-time team-lead post and rate three internal candidates, each on four 0-10 questions: would they recommend the candidate, and how do they see the candidate's work commitment, productivity and team-playing. Each candidate varies on gender (through the name and pronouns), parenthood, their own home working, how common home working is in the company, and the company's hybrid-working policy. The question the design asks is whether home working is stigmatised, and more so for mothers. Wave 16 (2023).

rows.title: Vignettes: measuring partner satisfaction with division of household labour
rows.description: Respondents imagine themselves in a couple and rate how satisfied they would be with how the housework is shared. Five dimensions are randomised: whose job is full or part time, whose hourly pay is higher, whether there is a child and its age, how the housework splits between them, and whether paid help is employed. The respondent is INSIDE the scenario -- the wording is "Imagine that you are married or cohabiting" -- so the outcome is imagined own satisfaction, not judgement of a described couple. Wave 5 (2012).
